intelligence.human_view: Before this, the unfold lived in three places and nowhere else: the pricing page's cover-to-chart walk, the agreement's board-by-board letter, the About page's story-by-story reveal. Each was built as if it were that page's idea. Shawn named what they share: a person should never face a wall of everything at once. One thing, understood, then the next thing, offered — never dumped. That is why the About button says the next section's name instead of "Keep reading" (15:36Z refinement): the unfold is a conversation, and a conversation names what comes next. The law changes every future brief: a page that presents everything at once is now a defect, not a style. The maker no longer asks "what goes on the page?" first; the maker asks "what unfolds first, and what does the person click to see next?" The About, the agreement, the walk-end, the pricing page — all four are now the same pattern wearing four different clothes, and the next page built joins them instead of inventing a fifth.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine a storybook that shows you the whole story on one giant page — all the pictures squished together, all the words at once. You wouldn't know where to start! Now imagine the storybook opens one beautiful page at a time — first the hero, then the adventure, then the treasure. Each page makes you smile, and you can't wait to turn to the next one. That's how every page should feel — one lovely surprise at a time!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — you don't serve the whole dinner in one big pile on the plate. You bring the soup, then the main, then the sweet — each one beautiful, each one in its turn, so the person enjoys every bite. A page is the same. Show them one lovely thing, let them take it in, then offer the next. That's how you make someone feel looked after, not overwhelmed.
intelligence.naya_view: I present one thing at a time, beautifully, and let the person ask for the next — because understanding arrives in steps, never in a pile.
